content: Eczema is a chronic dermatological condition characterized by dry skin, severe itching, and inflammatory lesions, which significantly affect patients' quality of life. Moisturizers are a cornerstone of eczema management, but their efficacy remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of moisturizers in treating eczema. A total of 77 randomized controlled trials involving 6,603 participants (mean age: 18.6 years) were included, with an average study duration of 6.7 weeks. The quality of evidence varied, with 36 studies at high risk of bias, 34 at unclear risk, and only seven at low risk. The primary outcomes assessed were participant-reported disease severity, satisfaction, and adverse events. Secondary outcomes included investigator-assessed disease severity, skin barrier function, flare prevention, quality of life, and corticosteroid use. Six studies compared moisturizers to no moisturizers. Moisturizer use was associated with lower SCORing Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) scores (mean difference [MD] -2.42, 95% confidence interval [CI] -4.55 to -0.28), although the minimal important difference (MID) was not achieved. Moisturizers reduced the frequency of flares (relative risk [RR] 0.40, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.70), prolonged the time to flare (median: 180 vs. 30 days), and decreased the use of topical corticosteroids (MD -9.30 g, 95% CI -15.3 to -3.27). Adverse events, such as stinging, itching, and erythema, were not significantly different between groups. Atopiclair, a specific moisturizer, demonstrated improvements in disease severity (RR 4.51, 95% CI 2.19 to 9.29), reduced itching (MD -2.65, 95% CI -4.21 to -1.09), and increased participant satisfaction (RR 2.14, 95% CI 1.58 to 2.89). It also lowered Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) scores (MD -4.0, 95% CI -5.42 to -2.57) and reduced flares (RR 0.18, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.31). However, the MID was not met. Adverse events were comparable to the control group. Urea-containing creams improved participant-reported skin condition (RR 1.28, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.53) and investigator-assessed dryness (RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.14 to 1.71). They also reduced flares (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.92) but caused more adverse events (RR 1.65, 95% CI 1.16 to 2.34). Glycerol-containing moisturizers were associated with improved skin condition (RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.48) and lower SCORAD scores (MD -2.20, 95% CI -3.44 to -0.96). However, participant satisfaction and adverse events were not significantly different from controls. Oat-containing moisturizers showed no significant differences in participant-reported disease severity, satisfaction, or investigator-assessed disease severity. However, they reduced flares (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.70) and corticosteroid use (MD -9.30 g, 95% CI -15.3 to -3.27) but were associated with more adverse events (Peto odds ratio 7.26, 95% CI 1.76 to 29.92). When comparing all moisturizers to placebo, vehicle, or no treatment, moisturizers were more effective in reducing eczema severity (RR 2.46, 95% CI 1.16 to 5.23) and itch (standardized mean difference [SMD] -1.10, 95% CI -1.83 to -0.38). Investigator-assessed disease severity scores were also lower (SMD -1.04, 95% CI -1.57 to -0.51), and flares were less frequent (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.62). Adverse events were comparable between groups. Combining moisturizers with active treatments was more effective than active treatments alone in reducing disease severity (SMD -0.87, 95% CI -1.17 to -0.57) and flares (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.93). Participants also preferred the combination therapy. Adverse events were not significantly different. In conclusion, most moisturizers demonstrated beneficial effects in managing eczema, including prolonging time to flare, reducing flare frequency, and decreasing corticosteroid use. Combining moisturizers with active treatments yielded better outcomes than active treatments alone. However, there is no reliable evidence to suggest that one type of moisturizer is superior to another.
